History:
• 50-year-old man feels “run-down” for ~5 days (onset Saturday).  
• Symptoms:  
  – Cough mainly dry, slightly worse in mornings; admits occasional “mucky” sputum.  
  – Runny nose/sniffles.  
  – Sore throat (also shouts at football).  
  – Mild ear dullness but no significant ear pain.  
  – Shortness of breath (“not good”) without chest pain.  
  – Subjective fevers/chills with night sweats; no temperature measured.  
  – 1 day of diarrhoea on first day, now resolved.  
  – Generalised myalgias/joint stiffness when bending elbows/knees.  
  – Appetite preserved; drinking extra fluids. No nausea or vomiting.  
• No clear trigger; no known COVID exposure discussed.  
• Similar episodes: none stated.

Past Medical History:
• Diabetes mellitus – patient first says “type 2,” then also says “type 1” (conflict noted).  
• Hypertension.  
• Overweight/obese (self-described).  
• Allergies: none known.  
• Medications:  
  – Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
  – Lisinopril (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
  – Occasional aspirin (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
• Social: Lives with wife; works in steel-parts factory. Drinks ≈9 pints beer/week. Occasional smoker, currently transitioning to vaping. Children grown and moved out.

Physical Examination:
• Tele-consultation; no vitals taken.  
• Audible cough and nasal congestion.  
• Patient alert and conversational.  
• No other physical findings recorded.

Impression:
Most consistent with an acute viral upper respiratory infection / influenza-like illness (including possible COVID-19).  
DDx consistent with transcript:  
1. Acute viral URI/influenza-like illness – matches abrupt onset, cough, rhinorrhoea, myalgias, subjective fever.  
2. Community-acquired pneumonia – less likely but considered due to sputum and dyspnoea.  
3. Acute bronchitis – alternative for sub-acute cough without focal chest findings.

Management Plan:
• Conservative care: rest, maintain hydration.  
• Antipyretic/analgesic: Paracetamol as needed for fever and soreness.  
• Delayed antibiotic prescription: Amoxicillin “one tablet three times daily” (dose/route not documented) to start if no improvement within 24–48 h or if symptoms worsen.  
• Safety-net advice: seek immediate care if breathing deteriorates, chest pain develops, high fever persists, or confusion occurs.  
• Follow-up: telephone or in-person re-assessment next week if not improving.  
• Lifestyle: continue efforts to stop smoking (vaping as bridge); moderate alcohol intake; monitor blood glucose regularly while ill.  
• Continue regular Metformin and Lisinopril.

Patient Summary:
Middle-aged man with diabetes, hypertension, and recent onset of cough, upper-respiratory symptoms, myalgias, and subjective fever most likely has a viral URI/flu. Given mild dyspnoea and minimal sputum, a watch-and-wait approach plus a delayed Amoxicillin script was provided, with instructions to rest, hydrate, and return if not better.

Key Takeaways:
• Start Paracetamol for fever/aches; keep well-hydrated and rest.  
• Use the Amoxicillin course only if still unwell or more breathless after 24–48 h.  
• Return immediately if breathing worsens, high fever develops, or new chest pain appears.

Next Steps:
• If no improvement, schedule in-person visit for full exam, vitals, and possible chest X-ray and viral testing.  
• Review diabetes and blood-pressure control at next routine visit.  
• Continue smoking-cessation support.
